A1.justification: Both PDFs describe VELOCITI, built from VidSitu movie clips and semantic role annotations. Their complete main texts, tables, figures, equations and appendices are readable. The substantial reframing and changed evaluation settings can be identified reliably.

before.justification: v1 Tables 2–3 report original evaluations of contrastive models, Video-LLMs, Gemini and humans on VELOCITI, supported by appendix annotation and dataset analyses.

after.justification: v2 reports original StrictVLE, ClassicVLE and multiple-choice evaluations, human results, and additional diagnostic experiments in the main text and Appendix A.

M1.justification: The retained tests use the same basic construction procedures: LLaMA-3 converts SRL dictionaries into captions, entities or actions are substituted, and templates construct coreference and chronology examples. No predictive architecture or training objective is introduced. StrictVLE changes the evaluation criterion, assessed under E3 and T1.

E1.justification: The VidSitu movie domain and seven caption tests remain, including Agent Identification renamed Agent Random and Action Modifier renamed Action Manner. However, v2 removes the separate Intra-Video Association Test using two cropped video segments and the text-to-video control task. The new input ablations use the retained benchmark.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated Qwen2-VL, LLaVA-OneVision, Gemini-1.5-Pro and GPT-4o models. Compared with v1 Tables 2–3, the ClassicVLE comparison in v2 Table 4 drops CLIP, EVA-CLIP, CLIP-ViP and mPLUG-Owl-Video rows while retaining several other comparators. Table 6 additionally evaluates a base language model and a single-image checkpoint.

E3.justification: v2 makes paired yes/no classification under StrictVLE primary, while retaining relative ranking as ClassicVLE and systematically testing both multiple-choice orders. Filtering changes the reported base from 900 videos and 4,500 event captions to 864 videos and 3,101 pairs. Human evaluation changes from five volunteers making retrieval judgments to three classifying individual video-caption pairs. Appendix B.3 also specifies subset selection through trials matching OV-72B performance, and new experiments vary prompts and frame sampling.

E4.justification: v2 adds extensive positive/negative decision analyses, quantified choice-order bias, blind-model and single-frame controls, chain-of-thought and frame-rate ablations, and scored success/failure cases (Sections 5.2–5.5 and Appendix A). These investigate response bias, dependence on visual and temporal inputs, and prompting sensitivity beyond v1's plausibility check and brief qualitative discussion of choice bias.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests for model performance. v2's scatter plots display individual examples' entailment scores, not estimates of experimental uncertainty.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive StrictVLE and diagnostic results, including subset averages of 44.5% for OV-72B, 49.3% for Gemini-1.5-Pro and 93.0% for humans (Table 2). Retained relative-ranking results also change: PLLaVA averages 55.3% in v1 Table 3 and 59.5% in v2 Table 4. These concern revised data/settings, not demonstrated same-setting model improvements. IVAT results are removed.

T1.justification: v2 Section 4 introduces the formal StrictVLE condition requiring positive-caption entailment above 0.5 and negative-caption entailment below 0.5, with 25% random accuracy. It adds a numerical counterexample demonstrating why relative ranking can accept incorrect yes/no responses. v1's IVAT matching and group-score definitions disappear; neither version contains substantial theorem or proof development.

C1.justification: v1 foregrounds a benchmark exposing perception and binding failures across contrastive and generative models. v2 makes StrictVLE a central contribution and focuses its primary evaluation on Video-LLMs. Its abstract and contributions also foreground action-versus-agent difficulty, shortcomings of ClassicVLE and multiple-choice evaluation, and the requirement for visual inputs spanning multiple frames.

C2.justification: v2 develops substantive explanations involving yes-response bias, nearly indistinguishable entailment scores, model-size effects and why simultaneous caption presentation makes multiple-choice evaluation easier. Appendix D explicitly limits StrictVLE's applicability to models supporting yes/no decisions. Human-centric scope and scaling limitations persist, while v1's discussion of societal stereotypes and the unexplored audio modality is removed.

D1.justification: v2 adds model-specific evaluation prompts, input details and an OV-7B runtime of approximately 2.6 hours on one RTX 4090 (Appendices B.6–C). However, it removes v1's datasheet documenting JSON distribution, a loading notebook, licensing and maintenance, and omits the earlier explicit decoding settings. This changes reproducibility documentation without establishing that the underlying resources became unavailable.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning through a comparative benchmark table and a dedicated entailment discussion. Newly discussed works include VITATECS, Vinoground, TVBench, TempCompass and NaturalBench. The distinction from prior work now emphasizes strict entailment and evaluation bias alongside in-video negation, rather than mainly contrasting perception with concept binding.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and much of the explanatory narrative are rewritten. Tests are regrouped around agents, actions, multiple events and negation strategies; StrictVLE receives a dedicated section. The appendices are extensively reorganized around results, benchmark construction, prompts and limitations, replacing the earlier prompts/annotation/statistics/datasheet structure.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from a predominantly single-column layout to two columns. v2 adds a Venn diagram, redraws the benchmark schematic, introduces extensive diagnostic tables and scatter plots, and presents scored qualitative examples. Appendix prompts are reformatted, dataset plots are revised, and a categorized action word cloud replaces the earlier frequency-chart presentation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evaluation validity and diagnostic value: StrictVLE and the score/choice-bias analyses expose errors hidden by v1's relative ranking, while blind and single-frame controls directly test the benchmark's dependence on video information. These gains outweigh reduced datasheet and access documentation. Important qualifications remain: Appendix B.3 conditions subset selection on OV-72B performance, and Table 9 labels its main-result OV-72B scores as 8fps despite the stated 1fps default, weakening the frame-rate interpretation.
